glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The Son into whose kingdom the Father has rescued His people is supreme in creation, the church, and reconciliation, so the reconciled Colossians are called to continue in the faith while Paul labors to present them mature in Christ.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Paul writes in chains (4:18), probably from Rome in the early AD 60s, to a church that learned the gospel from Epaphras (1:7). Epaphras's report of their "love in the Spirit" (1:8) prompted this chapter's thanksgiving and prayer.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: "And He is the head of the body, the church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things He may have the preeminence." (Colossians 1:18)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Colossians 1 moves from prayer into worship without changing subjects. Paul's prayer ends with the Father, who "has delivered us from the power of darkness and conveyed us into the kingdom of the Son of His love" (1:13). The very next lines tell who that Son is: "He is the image of the invisible God" (1:15), the One in whom the unseen God is made known. Paul says "all things" again and again in 1:16–20. All things were created by the Son and for Him, all things hold together in Him, and all things are reconciled through Him. The One who made the universe is also the head of the church and "the firstborn from the dead," so that "in all things He may have the preeminence" (1:18).

Behind the Son's supremacy stands the Father's delight. Paul writes that "it pleased the Father that in Him all the fullness should dwell" (1:19), so everything God is lives in the Son. Through that Son the Father made "peace through the blood of His cross" (1:20). This peace reaches across all creation. Read alongside 2:15, it includes hostile powers being disarmed and brought under Christ's rule, an outcome distinct from the reconciliation believers receive.

Then Paul says, "And you" (1:21). The peace that spans heaven and earth reaches people who "once were alienated and enemies." The God who placed His fullness in the Son now makes the Son known among Gentiles: "Christ in you, the hope of glory" (1:27). Throughout the chapter the Father takes the first step, and Paul's own suffering and labor serve to bring believers to maturity in that Christ.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Colossians 1:1–2 — Paul and Timothy Greet the Saints in Colosse

Paul writes as "an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God," with Timothy beside him, and he greets the church as "saints and faithful brethren in Christ" before he mentions any concern. He names "God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" together as the source of the grace and peace he wishes them.

Colossians 1:3–8 — Thanksgiving for the Gospel's Fruit Among the Colossians

Paul and Timothy thank God for the Colossians' faith in Christ Jesus and their love for all the saints, both growing from "the hope which is laid up for you in heaven" (1:5). The gospel Epaphras taught them is the same message "bringing forth fruit" throughout the world, and Paul's warm commendation of Epaphras confirms that what they first received was the true gospel.

Colossians 1:9–14 — Prayer for a Worthy Walk and Thanks for the Father's Rescue

Since hearing Epaphras's report, Paul has prayed that the church will be "filled with the knowledge of His will" so that they "walk worthy of the Lord," fruitful, strengthened by God's power, and thankful. Their thanks looks back to what the Father has already done: He rescued them from the power of darkness into His Son's kingdom, where they have "redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins" (1:14).

Colossians 1:15–20 — The Son Supreme in Creation, the Church, and Reconciliation

Paul declares that the Son is "the image of the invisible God," the Creator who also holds all things together, and the head of the church who has first place among all who are raised from the dead. Because all the fullness of God dwells in Him, the Father reconciles all things through Him, "having made peace through the blood of His cross" (1:20).

Colossians 1:21–23 — The Colossians Reconciled and Called to Continue in the Faith

With "And you," Paul brings that peace home to the Colossians, who were once God's enemies and are now reconciled through Christ's bodily death, so that He may present them holy and blameless in His sight. The promise comes with a condition Paul means seriously, "if indeed you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast" (1:23), and he ends the sentence by identifying himself as a minister of this same gospel.

Colossians 1:24–29 — Paul's Suffering and Labor to Make the Mystery Known

Paul rejoices to suffer for Christ's body, the church, as a steward God has entrusted with making His word fully known. That word is a mystery once hidden and now revealed among the Gentiles, "Christ in you, the hope of glory" (1:27), and Paul labors by God's own power to present every believer mature in Christ, a labor his account carries on into 2:1–5.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Colossians 1 settles who Christ is before Paul warns about the teaching that pressed on the church in chapter 2. Once a reader has seen the Son as Creator, sustainer, head of the church, and the dwelling place of all God's fullness, Paul's later claim makes sense: "you are complete in Him" (2:10). No rule or experience can add to the One in whom all things hold together.

The chapter also shows the order of the Christian life. The Father qualifies, delivers, and reconciles first, and His people respond with thanksgiving and growing fruitfulness.

Finally, Colossians 1 keeps the promise and the warning together. Christ reconciles His people in order to present them blameless, and Paul calls them to continue in the faith. God uses that real warning to keep His people steadfast, and their endurance rests on His grace.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The Son's preeminence (1:15–19). Paul places the Son first in creation, in the church, and in resurrection, and he grounds that first place in the fullness of God dwelling in Him.

Peace through the cross (1:20–22). Christ's death makes peace on the scale of creation and reconciles former enemies to God.

The Father acts first (1:3, 12–14, 19, 27). Thanksgiving answers what the Father has already done: He qualified His people, delivered them, and chose to make His mystery known.

The gospel bearing fruit (1:5–6, 9–10). The gospel bears fruit from the day it is heard, and Paul prays that the Colossians will keep bearing fruit as they grow in the knowledge of God.

Christ in you (1:26–28). God's once-hidden purpose is Christ living among Gentile believers as one people and in each of them personally, as their hope of glory.

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Firstborn (1:15, 18). The word speaks of first place in rank and authority. Paul calls the Son "the firstborn over all creation" and immediately explains, "For by Him all things were created" (1:16), which places the Son on the Creator's side. He is not the first thing God made. "The firstborn from the dead" names Him as the source of resurrection life and the highest among all who are raised.

Fullness (1:19). Here "fullness" means the complete divine nature. Paul says it outright in 2:9: "For in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily." Everything God is lives in the Son.

Reconcile and "all things" (1:20–21). To reconcile is to end hostility and make peace. Believers who were once enemies are brought back to God. Read with 2:15, the same peace includes hostile powers being disarmed and brought under Christ's rule. Their defeat is different from salvation, and the verse does not teach that every creature will be saved.

Thrones, dominions, principalities, powers (1:16). These are names for ruling powers, including unseen ones. However exalted they are, every one was created by the Son and for Him. This prepares for Paul's statement that Christ is "the head of all principality and power" (2:10).

Mystery (1:26–27). In Colossians a mystery is God's purpose, kept hidden in past ages and now openly revealed to all His saints. Its heart is "Christ in you, the hope of glory," made known among the Gentiles.

"What is lacking in the afflictions of Christ" (1:24). Paul is speaking of the sufferings that still fall to him as he serves the church. The precise sense of the phrase is debated. The safeguard, though, is clear: the same chapter says believers are reconciled "through death" (1:22), so Christ's atoning death lacks nothing.

focus: Colossians 1 moves from Paul's greeting, thanksgiving, and prayer for the church in Colosse into a sweeping declaration of the Son's supremacy over creation and the church, and then applies the reconciliation He accomplished to the Colossians themselves. The chapter closes with Paul's account of the suffering and labor his calling involves, an account that continues into 2:1–5.

1.brief: Paul opens by calling himself "an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God," so his authority to write rests on God's appointment, not on his own initiative. He names "Timothy our brother" beside him as a fellow believer who shares in the greeting.
1.explain:
Paul opens the letter with his own name. He is the same man who says later in this chapter, "I, Paul, became a minister" of the gospel (1:23), and who signs the closing greeting "by my own hand" (4:18). From its first word to its last, Colossians comes to the church as a personal letter from a man they could name.

an apostle of Jesus Christ describes the role in which Paul writes. An apostle of Jesus Christ belongs to Christ and is sent to speak for Him, so what follows comes with Christ's authority behind it. Paul is not offering the Colossians private advice. Later in the chapter he describes his calling as "the stewardship from God which was given to me for you" (1:25), a trust God placed in his hands for the good of churches like this one.

by the will of God tells where that role came from. Paul did not appoint himself or earn the title; God willed it. This matters for a church that first heard the gospel from Epaphras (1:7) and that may never have seen Paul's face (2:1). The Colossians can receive his words as a message from someone God Himself appointed, even though Paul did not found their church.

and Timothy our brother names the companion who stands with Paul as he writes. Paul gives Timothy no official title here. He calls him "our brother," a fellow believer, and that family language carries straight into the next verse, where the Colossians themselves are greeted as "faithful brethren." Because Timothy shares in the greeting, the thanksgiving and prayer that follow speak as "we" (1:3, 9). Paul still writes as the apostle, and the authority claimed in this verse belongs to him.
1.notes: The NLT renders the opening as "chosen by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus." This rendering spells out what the shorter NKJV wording implies: "by the will of God" describes how Paul came to be an apostle.

2.brief: Paul addresses the church as "saints and faithful brethren in Christ," calling them God's holy people and His faithful family before he raises any concern. He greets them with grace and peace from "God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ," naming the Father and the Son together as the source of these blessings.
2.explain:
To the saints names the Colossians by what God has made them. Paul uses the word for the whole congregation, not for a few believers of unusual achievement. Saints are God's holy people, set apart to belong to Him. The church's holiness begins with God claiming them as His own.

and faithful brethren adds the language of family. "Brethren" is an older English plural of "brother." Here it takes in the whole church as members of one household of faith. "Faithful" describes them as believers who are holding to the faith they received. Paul says all this before he raises any concern. His later warning, "lest anyone should deceive you with persuasive words" (2:4), is addressed to a church he has already greeted as holy and faithful.

in Christ tells why they are holy and faithful: they belong to Christ and share His life. Their standing rests in Him rather than in anything they add to Him. This short phrase prepares for one of the letter's central claims, that believers are "complete in Him" (2:10).

who are in Colosse gives the church's earthly address. The same believers who are "in Christ" also live in a real city among ordinary neighbors, and their life in Christ is lived out there. Colosse was not isolated, either. The letter later names believers in nearby Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13) and asks that this letter be read in the church of the Laodiceans as well (4:16).

Grace to you and peace is Paul's greeting and his prayerful wish for the church. Grace is God's undeserved kindness, the favor He gives freely. Peace is the well-being that comes from being at peace with God. Both words carry weight in this letter. Paul soon declares that Christ made peace "through the blood of His cross" (1:20), and he later urges the church, "let the peace of God rule in your hearts" (3:15).

from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ names the source of grace and peace. Paul places the Father and the Son side by side as the One from whom these blessings come. "Our Father" continues the family language of "brethren": the God who gives grace to this church is their Father. Calling Jesus "the Lord" acknowledges His authority, and Paul unfolds that authority within a few verses when he declares that "in all things He may have the preeminence" (1:18).
2.notes:
Translations differ at the end of this verse. The NLT reads "May God our Father give you grace and peace" and does not include the words "and the Lord Jesus Christ," which appear in the NKJV. In either wording, the very next verse gives thanks to "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1:3), so the letter's opening lines still join the Father to the Lord Jesus Christ.

Grace frames the whole letter. Paul opens with "Grace to you" here and closes in his own hand with "Grace be with you" (4:18).

3.brief: Paul and Timothy give thanks to "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" whenever they pray for the Colossians. Their prayer for this church begins with gratitude for what God has already done among them.
3.explain:
We give thanks to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is spoken by Paul and Timothy together, since Paul named Timothy beside him in the greeting. Before they ask anything for the Colossians, they thank God for them. Paul identifies the God he thanks by His relationship to Jesus: He is the Father of the One the Colossians confess as Lord. The thanks goes to the same Father who, as verses 12–14 will say, rescued His people and brought them into His Son's kingdom.

praying always for you shows that this gratitude belongs to a steady habit of prayer. Whenever Paul and Timothy pray for this church, thanks comes first, and their actual requests wait until verse 9. By starting this way, Paul lets the Colossians know that he already sees God at work among them. The rest of the sentence explains what he has heard.
3.notes: In the NKJV, verses 3–8 form one long sentence. It begins with thanks to God in verse 3 and does not reach a full stop until Epaphras's report in verse 8. The faith, love, hope, gospel, and messenger described along the way all belong to the same thanksgiving. Verse 9 then opens a new sentence with "For this reason."

4.brief: The thanksgiving was prompted by news of the Colossians' "faith in Christ Jesus" and their "love for all the saints." Their trust in Christ showed itself in a love that reached every believer, not only those close to them.
4.explain:
since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus gives the news that moved Paul and Timothy to thank God. They know about the Colossians' faith from a report; they did not watch it grow. That faith is "in Christ Jesus," meaning the Colossians have put their trust in Him. Their faith rests on a Person. That matters in a letter that will later tell them, "you are complete in Him" (2:10).

and of your love for all the saints names the evidence that this faith is genuine. "Saints" is the same term Paul used for the Colossians themselves in verse 2. It means God's holy people, everyone who belongs to Him. The Colossians' love did not stop with a favored few. It reached "all the saints," and that broad love showed that trusting Christ had changed how they treated His people.
4.notes: Paul received this news of the Colossians' faith and love through Epaphras, who "declared to us" their love (1:8). Later Paul writes of his struggle for "as many as have not seen my face in the flesh" (2:1). The letter does not say whether that group includes the Colossians, so whether Paul ever visited Colosse remains an open question.

5.brief: The Colossians' faith and love grow out of "the hope which is laid up for you in heaven," a future God is keeping safe for them. They first heard of this hope in "the word of the truth of the gospel," so their hope rests on a true message from God and not on wishful thinking.
5.explain:
because of the hope which is laid up for you in heaven explains where the Colossians' faith and love come from. In this phrase, "hope" means what is hoped for, not just a hopeful feeling. That hope is "laid up," meaning stored and kept, and it is kept "in heaven," beyond the reach of anything on earth. Faith and love grow from that secure future. People who know what God is keeping for them can trust Christ now and spend themselves in love for His people. Later in the letter Paul ties this hope to Christ Himself: "your life is hidden with Christ in God," and "When Christ who is our life appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory" (3:3–4).

of which you heard before in the word of the truth of the gospel reminds the Colossians when they first learned of this hope. They heard it "before," at the beginning, when the gospel first reached them. Verses 6–7 describe that day. What they heard was "the word of the truth of the gospel": the good news about Christ, a message that is true. Their hope stands on something God has spoken, not on guesswork or a teacher's clever ideas. Paul's stress on truth matters in Colossians, because he will soon write "lest anyone should deceive you with persuasive words" (2:4).
5.notes: The wording "which you heard" comes back in 1:23, where Paul urges the Colossians not to be "moved away from the hope of the gospel which you heard." The hope that supports their faith and love here is the same hope Paul later calls them to hold without drifting.

6.brief: The gospel that reached Colosse is the same message spreading "in all the world," and it is "bringing forth fruit" among the Colossians just as it does elsewhere. That fruit has been growing since the day they "heard and knew the grace of God in truth," meaning they understood and received God's grace as it truly is.
6.explain:
which has come to you makes the gospel itself the subject of the sentence. Paul speaks of the good news as if it were alive: it arrives, it spreads, and it bears fruit. The gospel came to Colosse. The Colossians did not work it out for themselves; they received it.

as it has also in all the world places that local arrival within a much larger movement. The message taught in this one church is the same message spreading across the world. Paul is describing how far the gospel has spread, not counting everyone who has heard it. For the Colossians, this means they hold the one gospel God is using everywhere, not a local or partial version of it.

and is bringing forth fruit, as it is also among you describes what the gospel does wherever it goes. Like a healthy plant, it produces fruit. In Colosse, that fruit is what Paul has just named: faith in Christ Jesus and love for all the saints (1:4). The words "as it is also among you" assure the church that the growth seen elsewhere is happening in their own fellowship too.

since the day you heard and knew the grace of God in truth traces that fruit back to its beginning. The gospel started working on the day it reached them, and the fruit has been growing ever since. "Heard and knew" means more than hearing words: they understood the message and took it to heart. What they came to know was "the grace of God," His kindness given freely to people who had not earned it. They knew it "in truth," as it really is, without distortion. Paul is telling the Colossians that their beginning was sound.
6.notes:
The words "since the day you heard" find an echo in verse 9: "For this reason we also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you." Two first hearings are set side by side. From the day the gospel reached Colosse, it bore fruit there. From the day news of their faith reached Paul, he and Timothy prayed for them without stopping.

The picture of fruit returns in Paul's prayer, where he asks that the Colossians be "fruitful in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God" (1:10). The fruit the gospel produced among them in verse 6 is the fruit Paul prays will keep growing in their daily lives.

7.brief: The Colossians learned this gospel from Epaphras, whom Paul calls "our dear fellow servant" and "a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf." By commending Epaphras, Paul confirms that the gospel they first received is the true one.
7.explain:
as you also learned from Epaphras names the man who first taught the Colossians the gospel. "Learned" points to real instruction. Epaphras did more than announce the message; he taught it until they understood it. Later Paul urges them to stay "established in the faith, as you have been taught" (2:7). What Epaphras taught them is the foundation Paul wants them to keep.

our dear fellow servant shows how warmly Paul regards Epaphras. He is "dear," loved by Paul and Timothy, and a "fellow servant," someone who serves the same Lord alongside them. Paul counts the Colossians' own teacher as a partner in his work.

who is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf adds Paul's formal endorsement. Epaphras serves Christ, and he has served faithfully. His ministry has been "on your behalf," for the good of the Colossians. By speaking of Epaphras this way, Paul confirms that the gospel the church received from him is the true gospel. Paul is not correcting their beginning; he is endorsing it.
7.notes:
Epaphras appears again near the end of the letter. Paul calls him "one of you," a man from the Colossians' own city, and "a bondservant of Christ" who is "always laboring fervently for you in prayers" (4:12). Paul adds that Epaphras has "a great zeal for you, and those who are in Laodicea, and those in Hierapolis" (4:13), so his care reached the neighboring churches as well.

Paul describes Tychicus in similar terms, calling him "a beloved brother, faithful minister, and fellow servant in the Lord" (4:7). Both men are called faithful ministers and fellow servants. Paul gives the same respect to the coworkers who carried the gospel and news between him and the churches.

The NLT ends this verse with "he is helping us on your behalf," which pictures Epaphras serving Paul in the Colossians' place. The NKJV reads "a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf," which describes his ministry as service done for the Colossians. In both translations Epaphras is a trusted servant linked to Paul and to the church.

8.brief: Epaphras also told Paul about the Colossians' "love in the Spirit," a love the Holy Spirit produces among them. This good report is what set Paul's thanksgiving and prayer in motion.
8.explain: who also declared to us your love in the Spirit completes the picture of Epaphras. He carried the gospel to Colosse, and he carried news of the church back to Paul. The news was about the Colossians' "love," the love for all the saints already mentioned in verse 4. Paul calls it "love in the Spirit," a love the Holy Spirit produces among them. Their love comes from the Spirit's work, not from natural friendliness alone. This report is what started Paul's thanksgiving, and in the next verse it moves him to steady prayer: "For this reason we also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you."
8.notes: This verse is the only place in the NKJV of Colossians where "Spirit" is capitalized. Elsewhere, "spirit" in 2:5 refers to Paul being present with the church in his thoughts, and the adjective "spiritual" describes understanding (1:9) and songs (3:16).

9.brief: Because of Epaphras's report, Paul and Timothy have not stopped praying for the Colossians since the day they heard it. They ask that the church be "filled with the knowledge of His will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding," which means knowing God's will together with the God-given insight to see how to live it.
9.explain:
For this reason we also, points back to the report Paul has just described. Epaphras had told him of the Colossians' "love in the Spirit" (1:8), and that good news led straight into prayer. The "we" includes Timothy, whom Paul named beside himself in the greeting (1:1). A healthy church did not make Paul feel that prayer was less needed. Good news about God's work moved him to ask God for more of it.

since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you, describes prayer that has continued without a break since the report arrived. Paul has already said that he and Timothy give thanks while "praying always for you" (1:3). Now he reveals what they have been asking. These are believers Paul came to know through another man's ministry, yet he carries them before God as faithfully as if he had planted the church himself.

and to ask that you may be filled with the knowledge of His will is the heart of the request. To be filled is to be full, with no corner left empty, so Paul wants knowledge of God's will to reach every part of the church's life. "His will" is what God desires and intends for His people. Later in the letter Paul warns against teaching that has only "an appearance of wisdom" (2:23). Before any warning is given, he prays that the church will be full of the real knowledge God gives, so that nothing else can claim to supply what is missing.

in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; describes the kind of knowledge Paul has in mind. Wisdom is the ability to apply God's truth rightly in real situations, and spiritual understanding is insight that comes from God's Spirit rather than from human cleverness. Paul is asking for more than information about what God wants. He wants the Colossians to see clearly how God's will applies to the choices in front of them, and the next verse shows what that knowledge is for.
9.notes: The NLT renders the request as "complete knowledge of his will" and "spiritual wisdom and understanding." Its word "complete" expresses the same fullness as the NKJV's "filled," and it applies "spiritual" to both wisdom and understanding. The meaning of the request is the same in both translations.

10.brief: Knowing God's will has a purpose: that the Colossians may "walk worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing Him." Paul describes that life as fruitful in every good work and "increasing in the knowledge of God," so faithful living and a deeper knowledge of God grow together.
10.explain:
that you may walk worthy of the Lord, gives the purpose of the knowledge Paul prayed for in verse 9. To "walk" is a common biblical way of describing a person's everyday conduct, the steady direction of a life. A walk "worthy of the Lord" is a life that fits who the Lord is and what He has done. Paul uses the same picture in 2:6: "As you therefore have received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in Him." Those words point to Christ as the Lord whose worth the Colossians' conduct should reflect.

fully pleasing Him, names the aim of that walk. Paul wants the Colossians to please the Lord in every area of life, not only in the parts others see. Knowing God's will is never an end in itself. It is given so that God's people can live in a way that delights the One they belong to.

being fruitful in every good work begins Paul's description of that worthy life. The gospel was already "bringing forth fruit" among the Colossians (1:6). Now Paul prays that the fruit will show up in actual deeds, and "every good work" takes in the whole range of ordinary goodness that comes from a life under Christ.

and increasing in the knowledge of God; completes the picture. In verse 9 Paul asked that they be filled with the knowledge of God's will. Here the knowledge goes deeper, to knowing God Himself. Knowledge leads to obedience, and the obedient life in turn grows in its knowledge of God, so the two keep growing together.
10.notes:
In the NKJV, the worthy walk is described by a chain of phrases that runs through verse 12: "being fruitful," "increasing," "strengthened" (1:11), and "giving thanks" (1:12). This chain explains why the thanksgiving of verse 12 belongs to Paul's prayer and does not begin a new subject.

Paul's language of knowing in this prayer reaches back to the Colossians' first hearing of the gospel, when they "knew the grace of God in truth" (1:6). The knowledge he asks God to increase began on that day.

11.brief: Paul prays that they will be "strengthened with all might, according to His glorious power," so the strength for a worthy life comes from God Himself. God gives that power "for all patience and longsuffering with joy," so that believers can endure hardship and bear with others without losing their joy.
11.explain:
strengthened with all might, continues the description of the worthy walk. Paul does not expect the Colossians to produce that life by willpower. They need to be strengthened, and the source of that strength is God. "All might" means every kind of strength the worthy life will require.

according to His glorious power, gives the measure of that strength. Believers are strengthened in keeping with God's own power, and not just with a little help from Him. His power is "glorious" because it displays who He is. The God whose glory is beyond measure supplies the strength His people need to live for Him.

for all patience and longsuffering with joy; reveals the surprising purpose of this power. Paul does not pray for spectacular displays. He prays for endurance. Patience is the strength to hold up under hard circumstances without giving way. Longsuffering is the strength to bear with difficult people without striking back, as Paul makes clear in 3:12–13, where "longsuffering" is followed by "bearing with one another." Paul adds "with joy," so the endurance he prays for is not grim. God's power is at work when His people keep going and keep loving, and still have joy.
11.notes:
The two translations place "joy" differently. The NKJV joins it to the preceding words: "patience and longsuffering with joy." The NLT ends verse 11 with "May you be filled with joy," and continues into verse 12 with "always thanking the Father," linking joy with thanksgiving. Either way, joy belongs to the worthy life Paul prays for.

Paul uses similar language about his own ministry at the end of the chapter, where he labors "according to His working which works in me mightily" (1:29). The strength he prays for the Colossians to receive is the same kind of divine working he relies on himself.

12.brief: The worthy life also includes "giving thanks to the Father," because He "has qualified us" to share in "the inheritance of the saints in the light." Believers have a place among God's people because the Father Himself made them fit for it.
12.explain:
giving thanks to the Father is the last mark of the worthy walk in Paul's prayer. Thanksgiving belongs to how the Colossians will live, alongside fruitfulness, growth in knowing God, and God-given endurance. Paul's own prayer began with thanks to the Father (1:3), and now he prays that the church will share that same gratitude.

who has qualified us gives the reason for the thanks. The Father has already made His people fit, and the action is complete. The Colossians did not qualify themselves, and they cannot add to what the Father has done. Paul says "us," placing himself beside the Colossians as one who also received this gift.

to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints tells what they were qualified for. To be a partaker is to have a real share. An inheritance is received as a gift, not earned as wages. "The saints" are God's holy people, the same word Paul used for the Colossians in his greeting (1:2). People who "once were alienated and enemies" (1:21) now have a full share alongside all of God's people.

in the light describes the realm where this inheritance belongs. Light stands for God's truth, purity, and presence, and it prepares for the contrast of the next verse, where the Father rescues His people from "the power of darkness." The inheritance belongs to the side of light, and the Father has placed His people there.
12.notes: The NLT reads "He has enabled you" where the NKJV reads "who has qualified us." Both translations include the Colossians among those the Father has made fit for the inheritance. The NKJV wording also includes Paul.

13.brief: Paul now gives the reason for that thanks: the Father "has delivered us from the power of darkness" and brought believers into "the kingdom of the Son of His love." Paul pictures salvation as a rescue from one ruling power and a transfer into the kingdom where the Father's beloved Son reigns.
13.explain:
He has delivered us from the power of darkness explains what the Father has done. "He" is the Father of verse 12, and the deliverance is a finished rescue. "The power of darkness" is the authority that sin and evil held over people before God rescued them. Paul is describing a real dominion, not just a gloomy state of mind. Believers did not escape on their own. The Father acted to set them free. Paul will soon show that every ruling power, "whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers," was created by the Son (1:16), and that at the cross He "disarmed principalities and powers" (2:15). The rescue Paul describes rests on that victory.

and conveyed us into the kingdom completes the rescue. God did not free His people and leave them without a home. He moved them into a new kingdom, under a new King. Salvation is pictured as a change of rule, and the change has already happened. Believers do not wait to belong to this kingdom; they belong to it now.

of the Son of His love, names the King. The kingdom belongs to the Son whom the Father loves. The people the Father rescues are brought under the reign of His beloved Son, and they are placed within the reach of the Father's love for Him. This phrase turns Paul's attention to the Son, who becomes the subject of everything that follows in verses 14–20.
13.notes: The NLT renders "the power of darkness" as "the kingdom of darkness," which makes the contrast between two kingdoms explicit. The NKJV's "power" puts the stress on the authority darkness exercised over people.

14.brief: In the Son believers "have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins," a release from the guilt of sin secured by Christ's death. This mention of the Son leads straight into Paul's declaration of who the Son is.
14.explain:
in whom we have redemption locates the believer's rescue in the Son. "In whom" refers to the Son of the Father's love, named at the end of verse 13. Redemption is release secured at a cost. The NLT expresses the cost by saying the Son "purchased our freedom." Paul says "we have" this redemption, so it is a present possession for everyone who is in the Son.

through His blood, names the price. The Son's blood means His sacrificial death on the cross. Paul returns to the same thought a few verses later, when he says the Father made peace "through the blood of His cross" (1:20). The release believers enjoy cost the Son His life.

the forgiveness of sins explains what this redemption means for believers. They are released from the guilt of their sins because God has forgiven them. Paul fills out this picture in 2:13–14, where God made believers alive, "having forgiven you all trespasses," and cancelled the record against them, "having nailed it to the cross." Having named the Son in whom forgiveness is found, Paul moves straight into telling who that Son is: "He is the image of the invisible God" (1:15).
14.notes: The NLT has no wording corresponding to the NKJV's "through His blood" in this verse. It reads, "who purchased our freedom and forgave our sins." Both translations speak of Christ's blood in 1:20, where the NLT says God made peace "by means of Christ’s blood on the cross."

15.brief: Paul declares that the Son is "the image of the invisible God," the One in whom the unseen God is made known. Calling Him "the firstborn over all creation" means He holds first place in rank and authority over everything made. As the next verse shows, it does not mean He was the first thing God created.
15.explain:
He is the image of the invisible God. Paul does not introduce a new subject here. The "He" is "the Son of His love" from 1:13, the One "in whom we have redemption" in 1:14, so the prayer flows straight into a declaration of who that Son is. God Himself cannot be seen; He is "invisible." Yet the Son is His "image," the One in whom that unseen God is shown and made known. Paul is not describing a partial likeness, because verse 19 will say that all the fullness of God dwells in the Son. To see the Son is to see what the invisible God is truly like.

the firstborn over all creation. The word "firstborn" could sound as though the Son were the first thing God made, but the next verse rules that out at once: "For by Him all things were created." The Son stands on the Creator's side of creation, not inside it as its earliest part. Here "firstborn" speaks of first place in rank and authority, and the word "over" fits that meaning. The Son holds the highest position over everything that has been made, and verse 18 will give Him the same title in His resurrection.
15.notes:
The NLT reads "Christ is the visible image of the invisible God." The word "visible" does not appear in the NKJV, but it draws out the contrast the verse already sets up: the God no one can see is made known in the Son.

The NLT renders the second line "He existed before anything was created and is supreme over all creation." That rendering spells out both ideas this passage attaches to "firstborn": the Son came before creation, and He rules over it. Verse 17 states the first idea directly in the NKJV: "He is before all things."

16.brief: The Son is supreme because "by Him all things were created," in heaven and on earth, seen and unseen, including every ruling power, "whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers." Everything was made "through Him and for Him," so the Son is both the Creator of all things and the One they exist for.
16.explain:
For by Him all things were created. The word "For" gives the reason the Son is firstborn over creation: He made it. "All things" leaves nothing outside His work. Whatever exists owes its existence to the Son, which is why He cannot be counted among created things.

that are in heaven and that are on earth, visible and invisible. Paul names two pairs that together cover everything. "In heaven" and "on earth" take in every place, and "visible and invisible" takes in every kind of being, including those no one can see. The unseen world is as much the Son's creation as the ground under the Colossians' feet.

whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. These four words are titles of rule and authority. Paul singles out these ruling powers, including unseen ones, because they are the very beings a person might be tempted to fear or honor. The teaching pressing on the Colossians included "worship of angels" (2:18), though the letter does not describe exactly what role it gave to such beings. Whatever their rank, every one of them was created by the Son, and Paul will later call Christ "the head of all principality and power" (2:10).

All things were created through Him and for Him. Paul repeats his opening claim and adds two further truths. "Through Him" means the Son is the One through whom everything came into being. "For Him" means creation exists for His sake and moves toward Him as its goal. The Son is both where creation came from and what it is for, so no power in heaven or on earth can stand beside Him as a rival.
16.notes: The NLT reads "such as thrones, kingdoms, rulers, and authorities in the unseen world," which ties the four titles to invisible powers. The NKJV places the list right after "visible and invisible" without assigning it to either realm. Colossians 2:15, where Christ "disarmed principalities and powers," shows that the letter has hostile powers in view, including unseen ones, but the NKJV wording leaves room for earthly rulers to stand under the same claim.

17.brief: The Son "is before all things," existing before everything created and ranking above it. When Paul says "in Him all things consist," he means the Son keeps holding the whole creation together, so the universe depends on Him at every moment.
17.explain:
And He is before all things. Paul says "He is," not "He was." The Son existed before anything was created, and He also ranks ahead of all of it. Both ideas belong to this phrase, and together they make plain what "firstborn over all creation" meant in verse 15. Everything else came into being at some point; the Son was already there.

and in Him all things consist. The word "consist" here carries the sense of holding together, as the NLT's "he holds all creation together" shows. The Son did not create the universe and then leave it to run on its own. He keeps holding it together, so the existence and order of creation depend on Him at every moment. The same Son who brought all things into being is the One who keeps them from falling apart.
17.notes: The NLT's "He existed before anything else" brings out the time sense of "before." The NKJV's "before all things" can describe either time or rank, and the context supports both: all things were created by the Son (1:16), and He holds first place over them (1:15, 18).

18.brief: The Son who rules creation is also "the head of the body, the church," the One who governs it and gives it life. As "the beginning, the firstborn from the dead," He is the source of resurrection life and holds the highest rank among all who are raised from the dead, so that "in all things He may have the preeminence," holding first place in creation, in the church, and in resurrection.
18.explain:
And He is the head of the body, the church. The same words that opened verse 17, "And He is," now turn from creation to the church. The Son who holds the universe together also rules His people. Paul calls the church a "body" and the Son its "head," the One who governs it and gives it life. Later in the letter Paul describes the body as "nourished and knit together" and growing from the Head (2:19). The church draws its life from Christ, and it answers to Him.

who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead. "The beginning" names the Son as the source of something new, and here that new thing is resurrection life. He was truly among the dead and came out from among them. As "the firstborn from the dead," He holds the highest rank among all who are raised. The title echoes verse 15: He is firstborn over the creation He made and firstborn in the life of resurrection.

that in all things He may have the preeminence. The word "that" states the purpose behind all of this. "Preeminence" means first place. The phrase "in all things" gathers up what Paul has said so far: the Son holds first place in creation, in the church, and in resurrection. There is nothing in which He takes second place.
18.notes: The NLT renders "the firstborn from the dead" as "supreme over all who rise from the dead." That wording reads the title as rank rather than simple sequence, the same meaning "firstborn" carries in 1:15.

19.brief: Paul gives the reason the Son holds first place: "it pleased the Father that in Him all the fullness should dwell." This fullness is the complete divine nature, as 2:9 states plainly, so everything God is lives in the Son.
19.explain:
For it pleased the Father. The word "For" introduces the reason the Son holds first place. Paul traces the Son's supremacy back to the Father's own good pleasure. The Son does not hold first place in competition with the Father. His preeminence is what the Father wanted and delighted to give.

that in Him all the fullness should dwell. Paul does not say here what "fullness" means, but he states it plainly in 2:9: "For in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily." The fullness is the complete divine nature. "All" leaves nothing out, so everything God is lives in the Son. To "dwell" is to live in a place as one's home, which means this fullness is not a passing visit. That is why the Son can be "the image of the invisible God" (1:15), and Paul will build on it when he tells the Colossians, "you are complete in Him" (2:10).
19.notes: The NKJV and NLT frame this sentence differently. The NKJV names the Father as the One who was pleased that the fullness should dwell in the Son. The NLT reads "God in all his fullness was pleased to live in Christ," making God in His fullness the subject who chooses to live in Christ. Both translations agree that the complete divine nature dwells in the Son by God's own pleasure.

20.brief: Through the Son the Father was pleased "to reconcile all things to Himself," on earth and in heaven, "having made peace through the blood of His cross." This peace reaches across all creation. Believers are reconciled to God, and, read together with 2:15, hostile powers are disarmed and brought under Christ's rule. Their defeat is a different outcome from salvation, and the verse does not teach that every creature will be saved.
20.explain:
and by Him to reconcile all things to Himself. Verse 19 ends with a comma, and this verse continues the same sentence. The Father who was pleased for all the fullness to dwell in the Son was also pleased to reconcile through Him. To reconcile is to end hostility and make peace. The need for reconciliation shows that something had gone wrong between God and His creation, and verse 21 names it plainly for the Colossians: they "once were alienated and enemies." The "all things" reconciled here are the same "all things" created in verse 16, so the reach of the Son's peacemaking matches the reach of His creating.

by Him, whether things on earth or things in heaven. Paul repeats "by Him" so that no reader misses who accomplishes this work. No other mediator shares it. Earth and heaven are both named again, as they were in verse 16, so no realm lies outside the reach of this peace.

having made peace through the blood of His cross. Here Paul says how the peace was made: through Christ's death. "Blood" points to His real, violent death, the same blood through which believers have "redemption" in 1:14. Verse 22 will say believers were reconciled "in the body of His flesh through death." The Son through whom all things were created made peace at a cross, a place of execution.

This peace does not have the same outcome for everyone it reaches. Believers are reconciled to God, as verses 21–22 go on to say. Read together with 2:15, where Christ "disarmed principalities and powers" and "made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them in it," hostile powers are disarmed and brought under Christ's rule. Their defeat is a different outcome from salvation. Paul describes peace made on the scale of all creation, and the verse does not teach that every creature will be saved.
20.notes:
The phrase "all things" appears six times in the NKJV of verses 16–20: twice in verse 16, twice in verse 17, once in verse 18, and once here. The repetition carries one subject from creation, through the Son's first place, to reconciliation, and it is a main reason these verses are read as a single unit.

The NLT makes the subject explicit: "through him God reconciled everything to himself." The NKJV carries the same sense by continuing the sentence from verse 19, where the Father is named as the One who was pleased.

21.brief: With "And you," Paul applies this reconciling work to the Colossians, who "once were alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works." Their hostility toward God showed in both their thinking and their deeds, "yet now" they have been reconciled.
21.explain:
And you — with these two words Paul brings the vast reconciliation of 1:20 down to the people reading his letter. He has just said that the Father was pleased "by Him to reconcile all things to Himself," whether things on earth or things in heaven. Now he tells the Colossians that this peace has reached them personally. The great claims about the Son describe what has already happened in their own lives.

who once were alienated — to be alienated is to be cut off and estranged. Before the gospel reached them, the Colossians stood outside any relationship with God, as strangers to Him. Most of them were probably Gentiles, which is why Paul later speaks of God's mystery made known "among the Gentiles" (1:27). The word "once" places that condition firmly in their past.

and enemies in your mind — Paul goes further than distance. The Colossians were enemies, actively opposed to God, and that hostility lived in their minds, in the way they thought and what they wanted. Their opposition to God was a settled outlook rather than an occasional lapse.

by wicked works — the hostility inside them showed itself in outward deeds. Their thinking and their actions belonged together. Paul describes their past plainly so the Colossians can see how complete the change in them has been.

yet now He has reconciled — everything turns on "yet now." Against their former alienation and hostility, God has acted. The reconciling is God's work through His Son, as Paul has just said in 1:19–20, and "has reconciled" describes something already done. Former enemies have been brought into peace with God, and the first move was entirely His. The sentence does not stop here. In the next verse Paul explains how this reconciliation took place.
21.notes:
In the NKJV, verse 21 ends in the middle of a sentence with "yet now He has reconciled." The people reconciled are the "you" named at the start of the verse. The NLT divides Paul's long sentence differently. It closes verse 21 with a complete sentence about the Colossians' former condition and opens verse 22 with "Yet now he has reconciled you to himself." The meaning is the same. The two translations simply arrange the wording differently around the verse division.

Paul uses the same pattern again in 2:13. He begins with "And you, being dead in your trespasses," describes their former condition, and then states what God did: "He has made alive together with Him." In 3:7–8 he likewise sets "in which you yourselves once walked" against "But now you yourselves are to put off all these." Colossians repeatedly sets the believers' past against what God has now done.

The NLT translates "alienated" as "far away from God" and presents "evil thoughts and actions" as what separated the Colossians from Him. The NKJV places their hostility "in your mind" and joins it with "wicked works." Both translations keep inner thought and outward conduct together.

22.brief: This reconciliation took place "in the body of His flesh through death," through Christ's real bodily death on the cross. Its goal is to present believers "holy, and blameless, and above reproach in His sight," standing before Him with no charge left against them.
22.explain:
in the body of His flesh through death — Paul now names how the reconciliation happened. It took place in Christ's own physical body, through His death on the cross. By naming both "body" and "flesh," Paul makes clear that he means a real human body that truly died. In 1:20 he said that peace was made "through the blood of His cross." Here he places that same work in the Son's actual body. God reconciled His enemies at the cost of His Son's real death in a human body.

to present you holy, and blameless, and above reproach — the reconciliation has a goal. God means to present these former enemies before Him in a condition that answers every part of their past. "Holy" means set apart as belonging to God. "Blameless" means without fault or defect. "Above reproach" means that no accusation against them can stand. People who were once hostile in mind and wicked in deeds are to be presented with nothing left to charge against them. In 2:14 Paul says that God has already dealt with the record against believers, "having wiped out the handwriting of requirements that was against us."

in His sight — this presentation takes place before God Himself, where nothing is hidden. The standard is God's own judgment rather than human opinion. Christ's reconciling death matters most in that place, because in God's sight no charge against His people remains.
22.notes:
The NKJV calls the One who reconciles simply "He" and does not name Him. The NLT also uses "he," but by naming the means as "the death of Christ in his physical body," its wording shows that the one reconciling is distinct from Christ. Identifying that subject as God is an inference from context, since in 1:19–20 the Father is pleased "by Him to reconcile all things to Himself," that is, through the Son. In either translation, the reconciliation happens through the Son's bodily death, as the verse states.

In the NKJV, "to present you" states a purpose, and the verse ends with a dash that carries the sentence into the condition in verse 23. The NLT expresses the same idea as a present result: "he has brought you into his own presence, and you are holy and blameless as you stand before him without a single fault." The NKJV wording keeps the goal and the "if" that follows it joined in one sentence.

23.brief: Paul attaches that hope to a real condition: "if indeed you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast," without drifting from "the hope of the gospel which you heard." The warning is meant seriously and calls believers to keep going in faith. Paul adds that this gospel has been "preached to every creature under heaven," describing how widely it has spread, and that he himself "became a minister" of it.
23.explain:
if indeed you continue in the faith — Paul now attaches a real condition to the goal he has just described. The Colossians must continue, which means they must keep remaining in the faith they first received through the gospel. Paul is not doubting them. In 2:5 he rejoices to see "the steadfastness of your faith in Christ." Still, he means the condition seriously. The hope of being presented blameless belongs to those who keep trusting Christ, and Paul wants the Colossians to hear that plainly.

grounded and steadfast — these two words describe what continuing looks like. "Grounded" pictures something resting on a firm foundation, and "steadfast" describes something that stays fixed in place. Faith that continues is settled and stable, because it rests on the gospel the Colossians received rather than on shifting opinions.

and are not moved away from the hope of the gospel which you heard — the danger is being moved off that foundation and gradually pushed away from what they first believed. The hope Paul means is the one he named at the start of the letter, "the hope which is laid up for you in heaven," which they "heard before in the word of the truth of the gospel" (1:5). They heard that gospel from Epaphras (1:7). This warning prepares for chapter 2, where Paul writes "lest anyone should deceive you with persuasive words" (2:4). To continue in the faith is to hold on to that same hope instead of trading it for something that promises more.

The warning comes alongside what this chapter says God supplies for endurance. Paul prays that the Colossians will be "strengthened with all might, according to His glorious power, for all patience and longsuffering with joy" (1:11). Presenting them blameless is God's own aim in reconciling them (1:22). God uses a real warning like this one to keep His people steadfast, and their endurance rests on His grace. Paul does not stop to answer every question later readers bring to this verse. He calls the Colossians to keep going.

which was preached to every creature under heaven — the gospel the Colossians heard is the same message proclaimed far and wide. Paul is describing how far it has spread, as he did in 1:6, where he said it had come to them "as it has also in all the world." He is not counting every individual who heard it. His point is reassurance. The gospel Epaphras brought to Colosse is the same gospel going out across the world, so the Colossians have no reason to exchange it for another.

of which I, Paul, became a minister — Paul ends the long sentence that began in verse 21 by naming himself a servant of this gospel. Here a minister is someone who serves. Paul serves a message that was entrusted to him. His personal stake in that message prepares for the next section, where he describes the suffering and labor his calling involves (1:24–29).
23.notes:
This clause is the first place in Colossians where Paul speaks of himself as "I." Up to this point the letter speaks as "we," as in "We give thanks" (1:3) and "we also" (1:9), because Paul includes Timothy in the thanksgiving and prayer. Here he writes "I, Paul," and his own calling and struggle stay at the center through 2:5.

The words "of which I became a minister" return in 1:25. There Paul describes himself as a minister of the church "according to the stewardship from God which was given to me for you." The repeated wording links the end of this section to the next one.

The NLT translates "the hope of the gospel which you heard" as "the assurance you received when you heard the Good News." It translates "preached to every creature under heaven" as "preached all over the world," which presents the phrase as a statement of how widely the gospel had spread. In 1:5 the NLT also speaks of the Colossians' "confident hope." Both of these NLT renderings present the hope as certain.

24.brief: Paul rejoices in his sufferings "for you," because they serve Christ's "body, which is the church." When he speaks of filling up "what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ," he means the sufferings that still fall to him in serving the church. Christ's atoning death lacks nothing.
24.explain:
I now rejoice in my sufferings for you — Paul has just named himself a minister of the gospel at the end of verse 23, and he turns at once to what that ministry is costing him. He writes in chains (4:3, 18), yet the first thing he says about his suffering is that he rejoices in it. "Now" sets his present hardship beside everything he has just said about Christ's reconciling work, and "for you" names the Colossians as the people his suffering serves. Paul does not delight in pain for its own sake. He rejoices because his hardships are doing good for believers who may never have seen his face (2:1).

and fill up in my flesh — "In my flesh" places the suffering in Paul's own body: the imprisonment, the chains, and the physical cost of his work. To "fill up" is to supply what is still needed to complete a measure. Paul sees his own body as the place where the hardship his calling requires is being borne.

what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ — This phrase needs the most care in the verse. Paul cannot mean that Christ's death left something undone. Just two verses earlier he says believers have already been reconciled "in the body of His flesh through death" (1:22), and in 2:14 he says the record against them was nailed to the cross. Paul is speaking about the sufferings that still fall to him as he serves the church, the share of hardship that belongs to his calling and is not yet complete. Readers debate exactly how these sufferings can be called "the afflictions of Christ," but the safeguard is plain: Christ's atoning death lacks nothing.

for the sake of His body, which is the church — Paul's suffering has a purpose beyond himself. He has already called Christ "the head of the body, the church" (1:18), and now he says his hardships serve that same body. Because the church is Christ's own body, suffering for the church is suffering in Christ's service. The NKJV ends the verse with a comma, and Paul's sentence runs straight on into the account of his calling in verse 25.
24.notes:
Within a few lines Paul uses "flesh" and "body" in two settings. In 1:22 Christ reconciled believers "in the body of His flesh through death," His own physical body on the cross. In 1:24 Paul suffers "in my flesh" for "His body, which is the church." The repeated words link the two verses, while the context keeps Christ's death, which has already reconciled believers, distinct from Paul's continuing service to the church.

The NLT renders the central clause, "I am participating in the sufferings of Christ that continue for his body, the church." That translation reads the phrase as Paul's share in sufferings that continue among Christ's people, where the NKJV keeps the wording "fill up ... what is lacking."

25.brief: Paul became a minister of the church through "the stewardship from God which was given to me for you," a responsibility God entrusted to him for the good of believers like the Colossians. His task is "to fulfill the word of God," making God's message fully known.
25.explain:
of which I became a minister — "Of which" points back to the church at the end of verse 24. In verse 23 Paul said he "became a minister" of the gospel. Here he says he became a minister of the church. The two belong together: Paul serves both the message and the people that message gathers into Christ's body. The next phrase explains how this role came to him.

according to the stewardship from God — A steward is a trusted servant put in charge of a household on its owner's behalf. Paul understands his ministry in those terms. The work belongs to God, and Paul is responsible for managing faithfully what God has placed in his hands. The words "from God" make clear that this charge, like his apostleship "by the will of God" (1:1), rests on God's appointment rather than on Paul's own initiative.

which was given to me for you — God gave the stewardship to Paul with a purpose. It was given "for you," for the good of believers like the Colossians, Gentiles who were once alienated from God (1:21, 27). That is why Paul can write with personal responsibility to a church that first learned the gospel from Epaphras (1:7).

to fulfill the word of God — Paul now names the goal of his stewardship. To "fulfill" the word of God here means to make God's message fully known, carrying it to its complete extent among the people God has sent him to serve. Paul's task is faithful and complete proclamation of what God has spoken. Verse 26 goes on to name what that word contains.
25.notes: The NLT renders the purpose clause as "proclaiming his entire message to you." That translation reads "to fulfill the word of God" as full and complete proclamation. The same concern appears when Paul later asks for prayer "that I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak" (4:4).

26.brief: The word Paul makes known is "the mystery which has been hidden from ages and from generations." Here a mystery means God's purpose kept hidden in past ages, which "now has been revealed to His saints" and is open to all God's people.
26.explain:
the mystery — Paul now names the word of God he was entrusted to proclaim. In everyday English a mystery is a puzzle to be solved or a secret kept from outsiders. Paul uses the word differently. In Colossians a mystery is God's purpose, once hidden and now disclosed by God Himself. People could not have worked it out on their own, and God has chosen to make it known.

which has been hidden from ages and from generations — "Ages" and "generations" describe long stretches of time and the people who lived through them. Across all those years God's purpose remained hidden, and generation after generation passed without seeing it made known.

but now has been revealed — "But now" marks the turning point. What God kept hidden He has now uncovered, and Paul's stewardship is to make that revelation known. The disclosure is God's act, and Paul's role is to proclaim what God has revealed.

to His saints — The mystery has been revealed to "His saints," the same word Paul used for the Colossians in his greeting (1:2). God's revealed purpose belongs to all His holy people. Paul will soon say that he preaches it to "every man" (1:28), so this mystery is open truth for the whole church, not knowledge held back for a few.
26.notes:
The movement from "hidden" to "but now has been revealed" follows the same pattern as 1:21, where the Colossians "once were alienated" and "yet now" are reconciled. In both verses Paul sets the former situation beside what God has now done.

The word "hidden" returns in 2:3, where Paul says that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." Colossians 2:2 also speaks of "the knowledge of the mystery of God." These verbal links tie Paul's account of his ministry here to his continuing explanation in 2:1–5.

27.brief: God chose to make known "the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles," and Paul names its heart: "Christ in you, the hope of glory." Christ now lives among Gentile believers as one people and in each of them personally, and His presence is their assurance of the glory still to come.
27.explain:
To them God willed to make known — "Them" refers to the saints of verse 26. The revelation of the mystery began with God's own will. People did not search it out. The same God whose will made Paul an apostle (1:1) chose to make this purpose known, and the initiative belongs to Him.

what are the riches of the glory of this mystery — Paul gathers words of wealth and splendor to describe what God has disclosed. The mystery holds "riches," and those riches belong to its "glory," the display of God's own greatness. Paul presents what God has made known as abundant and glorious, with nothing small or partial about it.

among the Gentiles — God has made His purpose known among the Gentiles, the nations outside Israel. The Colossian believers were probably mostly Gentiles, people who "once were alienated and enemies" (1:21) and whom Paul later describes as dead in "the uncircumcision of your flesh" (2:13). God's hidden purpose included people like them, and their church is evidence that it has now been revealed.

which is Christ in you — Paul names the heart of the mystery: Christ Himself dwelling in His people. Paul is writing to a church, and in the setting of "among the Gentiles," these words speak of Christ present among Gentile believers as one people. They are also personal, because Christ lives in each believer who belongs to Him. The church shares one life in Christ, and each member knows His presence for himself or herself. At its center the mystery is a Person, and He has come to live with His people.

the hope of glory — Christ's presence now is the pledge of glory still to come. Paul has already spoken of "the hope which is laid up for you in heaven" (1:5), and he later writes, "When Christ who is our life appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory" (3:4). The Christ who lives among and within believers today assures them that they will share His glory when He appears.
27.notes:
The NLT makes the Gentile address explicit: "the riches and glory of Christ are for you Gentiles, too." It renders "the hope of glory" as "This gives you assurance of sharing his glory," which treats hope here as confident expectation.

"Glory" appears twice in the verse, first in "the riches of the glory of this mystery" and then in "the hope of glory." The glory God has already displayed in revealing the mystery is joined to the glory His people still await.

28.brief: Christ Himself is Paul's message: "Him we preach," warning and teaching "every man in all wisdom." Paul aims to "present every man perfect in Christ Jesus," meaning mature in Christ. His repeated "every man" shows that this message is for all believers, not for a privileged few.
28.explain:
Him we preach — Because the mystery is "Christ in you," the message Paul proclaims is Christ Himself. In the NKJV "Him" stands first in the sentence, placing Christ at the center of the preaching. The "we" includes those who share the work with Paul, such as Timothy, who is named in the greeting (1:1).

warning every man and teaching every man — Preaching Christ involves two activities. Warning confronts danger and calls people back from wrong paths, which suits a letter that cautions believers against being deceived "with persuasive words" (2:4) or cheated "through philosophy and empty deceit" (2:8). Teaching builds understanding of the truth. Paul does both, and he does both for "every man," meaning every person without distinction.

in all wisdom — Paul's warning and teaching draw on the same wisdom he prayed the Colossians would receive, "all wisdom and spiritual understanding" (1:9). In this letter, true wisdom is found in Christ, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (2:3).

that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus — This is the goal of the whole ministry. "Perfect" here means complete or mature, fully grown in Christ. "Present" recalls 1:22, where Christ's death aims "to present you holy, and blameless, and above reproach in His sight." Paul's preaching and teaching serve the same purpose Christ's reconciling death has in view. The threefold "every man" leaves no believer out and reserves maturity for no inner circle. That maturity is "in Christ Jesus": believers grow by remaining joined to Him, the One in whom they are already complete (2:10).
28.notes:
The NKJV's "every man" uses "man" in the sense of each person, and the NLT renders it "everyone." The NLT also renders the goal as "present them to God, perfect in their relationship to Christ," reading "perfect" as maturity in relationship to Christ rather than flawless conduct.

The phrase "in all wisdom" appears again in 3:16, where the whole church is to let the word of Christ dwell in them richly "in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another." The teaching Paul describes as his own ministry here is later given to the believers as a work they share with one another.

Epaphras prays toward the same goal in 4:12, "that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God." Paul's labor and Epaphras's prayer aim at the Colossians' maturity.

29.brief: To reach that goal Paul works hard, "striving according to His working which works in me mightily." His effort is real, but the power behind it is God at work in him, and this labor continues into the "great conflict" for the churches that Paul describes in 2:1.
29.explain:
To this end — "This end" is the goal Paul has just named: presenting every person mature in Christ. His effort has a definite aim.

I also labor — Paul moves from "we" in verse 28 back to "I" and speaks of his own share in the work. To labor is to work hard. For Paul, ministry involves real toil and real cost, the same cost he has described as suffering in verse 24.

striving — Paul describes his work as a struggle, effort exerted against resistance. This struggle does not end with the chapter. In the next verse he writes, "For I want you to know what a great conflict I have for you" (2:1).

according to His working which works in me mightily — Paul's effort is real, but its strength comes from God. "His working" is divine power, and it "works in me mightily." Paul prayed that the Colossians would be "strengthened with all might, according to His glorious power" (1:11), and now he describes that same kind of power at work in his own ministry. He works hard because God is working powerfully in him, and his striving rests on that power rather than on his own reserves.
29.notes:
The NKJV keeps a repetition in "His working which works in me," naming the divine activity twice. The NLT renders the phrase "depending on Christ's mighty power that works within me," identifying the power as Christ's. Colossians speaks both of "the working of God, who raised Him from the dead" (2:12) and of "Christ in you" (1:27), so neither rendering moves outside the letter's own language.

Chapter 1 ends in the middle of Paul's account of his ministry, which runs on through 2:5. The book's larger movement continues to 2:5, and the following movement begins with the appeal in 2:6.
